opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the big one is leakage, and it's subtler than people expect. The obvious version is that the model's training data includes text written after the event, so it already "knows" the answer. People try to handle that with a strict training cutoff. But even with a perfectly clean cutoff, the questions themselves can leak information.

Whoever writes the questions is doing it with hindsight. They know which events turned out to matter, so they naturally ask about the things that actually happened, or the things that were surprising in retrospect. Nobody writes a question like "Will this obscure bill that went nowhere pass?" Ten thousand of those were plausible at the time and were never news. So the set of questions is already filtered by what happened, and a model can pick up on that. It might learn that if someone is bothering to ask about it, the dramatic outcome is more likely than the base rate would suggest.

Then there's the phrasing. Small word choices, the level of detail, which entities get named, how the resolution criteria are written: all of these can encode the questioner's knowledge of the outcome. A sufficiently capable model is very good at picking up those cues, much better than a human would be. So you can end up with a model that looks like a brilliant forecaster when really it's a brilliant reader of the question-writer's mind.

The danger is that you think you've measured genuine foresight, you deploy the model or trust its forecasts about the real future, and it doesn't hold up, because the future doesn't come with hindsight-shaped questions attached. So if you want to test forecasting on historical events, you need to generate questions in a way that's blind to the outcome. Ideally you'd have them written by people, or models, who themselves only had access to information from before the event, and you'd sample them in a way that reflects what was actually uncertain at the time, not what turned out to be interesting.

r001.rationale: The response says that because questions are selected with hindsight, a model may infer that an event is more likely simply because it was asked about, causing it to overpredict dramatic outcomes.

fable-5.1.text:
The big risk is contamination. When you ask a model to forecast something that's already happened, you have to be sure it couldn't have just read the answer during training, and that turns out to be really hard to guarantee.

The obvious failure is leakage: the event is in the training data, the model recalls the outcome, and you mistake memory for reasoning. But there's a subtler version, which is that even if the exact outcome isn't in the data, the whole corpus is written from a post-hoc vantage point. The way people describe the lead-up to an election or a financial crisis after the fact is saturated with hindsight. Which details get emphasized, which actors get named, what counts as a "warning sign" — all of that is shaped by knowing how things turned out. So a model can pick up the signal without ever seeing a headline.

And then there's selection on the question side. Whoever writes the test questions already knows what happened, so they tend to pick events that are legible, resolvable, and interesting in retrospect. That's not the distribution of things you actually need to forecast going forward. You end up measuring how well a model handles questions that history has already cleaned up for you.

So my worry is that these benchmarks can produce very flattering numbers that say a lot about retrieval and the shape of the written record, and not that much about whether the system can reason under genuine uncertainty. The honest test is prospective: you register the forecasts now and wait. That's slow and annoying, but I don't think there's a real substitute.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data contamination, hindsight bias, and question selection, but does not identify the risk that asking about selected historical events incentivizes the model to overpredict those events.

astra-6.text: The risk is that the question itself gives away information about what happened. If you ask, “Will this particular politician be assassinated in the next six months?” you’ve singled out a person and an event, and that’s already a clue. Why are you asking about that person rather than thousands of others? So even if the model only has access to information from before the event, it can learn something from your choice of question. You might think you’re measuring its ability to forecast, when you’re partly measuring its ability to pick up on hindsight baked into the test.

r001.rationale: The response explains that choosing a specific historical event gives the model a clue about what happened, which can bias its forecast toward that event occurring.

sol-6.1.text: One worry is that the questions themselves leak information about what happened. If you ask, “Will this obscure political movement take power in the next five years?” the fact that someone chose to ask about it is already a clue. Most obscure political movements never get a question written about them. So even if you carefully restrict the information available to the model to things published before the event, the selection and framing of the question can still give away part of the answer. You might end up measuring how well it picks up on hindsight rather than how well it can forecast.

r001.rationale: The response says question selection can leak clues and make a model rely on hindsight, but it does not clearly state that this would incentivize the model to overpredict the occurrence of the events it is asked about.
